idiom_name: value-semantic wrapper: std::unique_ptr<Letter> member plus virtual clone()
implementation_notes: The classic Coplien envelope (raw Letter* member, operator-> forwarding, hand-written copy constructor, assignment and destructor) collapses into a std::unique_ptr<Letter> member for ownership plus a virtual clone() for copying: the envelope stays an ordinary value type that can be copied and stored in containers, while the letter stays polymorphic. Since C++11 the clone idiom returns std::unique_ptr<Letter> so ownership is unambiguous and no leak is possible at a throw site; std::shared_ptr is the alternative when a copy is meant to share an immutable letter, and since C++17 a closed set of letters can be a std::variant, which replaces the dispatch with visitation and needs no allocation at all. Keep the hand-written envelope when the letter set is open (plugins, runtime swap) or must stay behind a compilation firewall; prefer the variant when the set is closed.
pitfalls: A unique_ptr member makes the envelope move-only, so forgetting the copy constructor (or writing one that copies the pointer, which will not compile) is the first surprise; a shared_ptr member instead shares a mutable letter between copies, which is the opposite failure.
The letter's destructor must be virtual, otherwise deleting through Letter* - which is exactly what unique_ptr<Letter> does - is undefined behaviour.
clone() cannot return a covariant unique_ptr<Derived>: smart-pointer types are unrelated, so the concrete type is erased at the clone boundary and callers that need it must downcast.

variants.name: Coplien envelope (raw letter pointer, operator-> forwarding)
variants.idiom_name: hand-written Envelope over Letter* with operator-> and a rule-of-three copy policy
variants.implementation_notes: The form Coplien documented: the envelope holds a raw Letter* and either repeats one stub per operation or overloads operator-> so calls read as if the envelope were the object; copying requires a virtual clone() called by a hand-written copy constructor, assignment and destructor (the rule of three). Choose it when the envelope must stay non-owning (borrowed letters), when the operator-> syntax is part of an existing API, or when a pre-C++11 toolchain must be supported; otherwise the unique_ptr form removes the manual lifetime management.
pitfalls: With a raw pointer the envelope cannot tell a borrowed letter from an owned one, so two envelopes holding clones of the same pointer (or one borrowed letter) produce a double delete or a dangling accessor.
operator-> forwarding exposes the letter's whole interface, including operations the envelope was supposed to hide, and breaks the moment the letter has no operator-> of its own.

variants.name: Concept/Model type-erasure envelope (letters share no base class)
variants.idiom_name: internal Concept/Model hierarchy holding any conforming letter
variants.implementation_notes: When the realizations are unrelated third-party types, lambdas or classes that cannot be given a common base, the letter interface is synthesized inside the envelope: a nested Concept declares the operations and a Model<T> template implements it by delegating to a stored T, while the outer value type holds a unique_ptr<Concept> and clones through Concept::clone(). This is the standard-library technique behind std::function; it keeps the envelope copyable and polymorphic at the price of one template constructor, an internal hierarchy and a header-only implementation.
pitfalls: The template constructor hijacks overload resolution if it is unconstrained, so copies of the envelope can be wrapped instead of copied - constrain it (requires/SFINAE) or provide a copy constructor that wins.
Const-correctness must be carried through the Model: a letter whose operation is non-const forces the Concept method to be non-const, which in turn makes the envelope's operation non-const.
A type-erased envelope cannot be inspected, so any behaviour that needs to compare or serialise the concrete letter must be part of the Concept - type-erasure is one-way.
